part_title: Start Here — Your AI Practitioner Learning Journey
review_basis: Personally reviewed original local WebPs module-00 slides 01–04, matching four visual-map lessons. Beginner-first orientation and real-life invoice decisions.

scenes.title: Your AI Practitioner learning path
scenes.narration: Welcome to AWS Certified AI Practitioner. This course begins from zero. You do not need to be a programmer or to have used Amazon Web Services before. Look at the four stages across the picture. On the left, Understand means learning what artificial intelligence, machine learning and cloud computing actually are. Artificial intelligence, or AI, is the broad idea of making computer systems perform tasks that usually need human intelligence. Machine learning, or ML, is a common way to build AI by teaching a system patterns from examples. Cloud computing means using computing services over a network instead of owning every server yourself. Next is Explore. Here you will meet models, prompts and AWS services. A model is the system that produces a prediction or generated response. A prompt is the instruction or question you give a generative model. The third stage, Evaluate, asks whether the result is useful, accurate, safe, fair and worth its cost. The fourth, Apply, is about choosing a solution and explaining why. Follow the glowing road at the bottom: learn the concept, see an example, and explain the decision. Imagine a college office receiving hundreds of emails. We might teach a system to classify the messages and route them to the right team, but we must still check whether it makes mistakes. In this course, knowing when NOT to use a complicated AI model is just as valuable as knowing when to use one. By the end, you should be comfortable explaining an AI choice to a classmate, colleague or customer in plain language.

scenes.title: From a business need to an AI choice
scenes.narration: Let's follow the three big numbered panels from left to right. The first shows a pile of invoices. An invoice is a document stating what was bought, how much each item costs, and the total amount owed. Imagine an accounts team that receives a hundred scanned invoices each day and wants to copy the totals into a spreadsheet. That is the business need. In panel two, the machine scans a document and extracts information. We are choosing a capability called document extraction, not automatically asking a chatbot to invent a paragraph. AI can help recognize printed text and locate fields such as the invoice number and total. The third panel shows an extracted total of one thousand four hundred fifty-eight dollars and seventy cents and a displayed confidence of eighty-seven percent. Confidence is an indication from the system, not proof that the number is correct. If the invoice total is wrong, somebody could pay the wrong amount. So the checklist asks about accuracy, human review and cost. A human may need to check uncertain invoices, especially when prices or tax calculations do not match. Along the bottom are three habits to carry into every lesson: explain the concept, select a suitable service, and recognize risk. Risk means what might go wrong, such as exposing private invoice information, returning the wrong amount, or choosing a service that costs more than it saves. Here is our first quick decision: if a company wants to extract invoice totals, should we begin with open-ended story generation or document extraction? Document extraction fits the task better. Always begin with the requirement, not the most fashionable technology.

scenes.title: Understand the role before the tools
scenes.narration: This slide is divided into a large left panel, foundational understanding, and a right panel, implementation depth comes later. On the left, first recognize AI and ML concepts. The small circle connects data, algorithms, models and predictions. Data is the information we learn from. An algorithm is a procedure a computer follows. A model is what applies learned patterns to a new input. A prediction is the resulting estimate or classification, such as whether an email is spam. Next, choose suitable AWS capabilities. AWS offers different services for machine learning, generative AI and data analytics. You do not have to memorize every service before understanding the problem it solves. Below, the colored gauge introduces precision and recall, two ways to judge a classifier. Precision asks: of the items we flagged, how many really were positive? Recall asks: of all truly positive items, how many did we find? The numbers point nine two and point seven eight on the slide are sample measurements. Imagine flagging suspicious bank transactions. Precision helps avoid too many false alarms. Recall helps avoid missing genuine fraud. We will learn the formulas later. The shield panel adds responsible AI and security: fairness, privacy, preventing harmful use and following organizational rules. Finally, look right. Writing model-training code, constructing full machine-learning pipelines and operating complex infrastructure are deeper skills for later stages. This foundational exam focuses more on explaining and selecting technology than on building it from scratch. What matters first is knowing why accuracy, data privacy and business value influence a technology decision.

scenes.title: AWS certification learning path
scenes.narration: The final orientation slide shows four AWS certification categories across the top: Foundational, Associate, Professional and Specialty. Foundational is where AI Practitioner belongs. It is designed to validate essential concepts and does not require prior professional cloud experience. Associate certifications generally focus on skills for a particular technical role. Professional certifications go deeper into advanced architecture or operations. Specialty credentials focus on particular areas, with availability and names depending on AWS's current certification catalog. The arrows are a learning illustration, not mandatory prerequisites. You do not need to pass every box in order. In the lower left, this course's goals are to recognize suitable AI services, use AI responsibly, and build a foundation for further learning. On the lower right, the student chooses a job goal after finishing AI Practitioner. Someone interested in designing applications might study architecture next. Someone who wants to work with data might focus on analytics or machine learning. And someone entering a non-technical business role can still use this knowledge to evaluate AI projects and explain requirements. Think of the certification as evidence of foundational understanding, not a guarantee of employment or expertise in all AWS services. A quick check: does passing AI Practitioner mean you must now complete an Associate exam? No. The next step depends on the kind of work you want to do. That completes our orientation. The next module explains what artificial intelligence actually is through practical examples before introducing specific tools.
